docs.title: parse_file_index()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_file_index(idx_value):

Description: Extracts the first integer match from an arbitrary file index representation returned by an LLM. It tolerates integer literals, composite annotations such as "3 # path/to/file.py", and range notation strings like "0-3", returning the leading integer while delegating range expansion to caller routines.

Parameters:

  • idx_value (Any): The raw value returned by the model representing a file index.

Returns:

  • int | None: The first parsed integer from the input value, or None if no numerical digits are present.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions internally; non-numeric strings or incompatible types safely yield None.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def parse_file_index(idx_value):
    nums = re.findall(r"\d+", str(idx_value))
    return int(nums[0]) if nums else None

The function converts the input argument to a string and executes a regular expression search for contiguous digit runs. If at least one digit sequence is discovered, the leading match is cast to an integer and returned. If no matching digits exist, it safely returns None.

docs.title: parse_file_indices()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_file_indices(idx_value) -> list[int]:

Description: Strictly validates and parses an index specification entry returned by an LLM into a concrete list of integer file indices. Unlike parse_file_index(), this function enforces strict syntactic rules: it rejects boolean values, discards negative integers, strips inline comment annotations, and evaluates bounded ascending ranges (supporting separators -, .., –, or to). Any string containing embedded prose, negative offsets, or file paths with numbers is rejected and returns an empty list to prevent mapping errors.

Parameters:

  • idx_value (Any): The raw index object (integer, string, or boolean) returned from an LLM payload.

Returns:

  • list[int]: A list containing the parsed file indices. Single indices produce a one-element list, valid ascending ranges are expanded into a sequence of consecutive integers, and invalid inputs return an empty list.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions. Invalid, negative, or malformed values are silently filtered to an empty list.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def parse_file_indices(idx_value) -> list[int]:
    if isinstance(idx_value, bool):
        return []
    if isinstance(idx_value, int):
        return [idx_value] if idx_value >= 0 else []
    text = str(idx_value) if isinstance(idx_value, str) else ""
    single = _INDEX_RE.match(text)
    if single:
        return [int(single.group(1))]
    span = _INDEX_RANGE_RE.match(text)
    if span and int(span.group(1)) <= int(span.group(2)) and int(span.group(2)) - int(span.group(1)) < 10000:
        return list(range(int(span.group(1)), int(span.group(2)) + 1))
    return []

The function performs explicit type discrimination. Booleans are rejected immediately to prevent Python's boolean subclassing rules from treating True as 1. If passed an integer, non-negative values are wrapped in a list, while negative values yield an empty list. For string representations, the input is evaluated against _INDEX_RE to match single indices with optional trailing comments; if matched, the single integer is returned. If that fails, it evaluates _INDEX_RANGE_RE to identify ranges separated by hyphens, periods, en-dashes, or the word "to". When a valid ascending span with a distance of fewer than 10,000 items is matched, range() generates the full inclusive integer sequence.

docs.title: load_prompt_template()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def load_prompt_template(template_name, advanced_mode=False, mode=None):

Description: Resolves and reads a Markdown prompt template from the project's prompts/ hierarchy on disk. The directory path is determined dynamically based on the execution mode parameter or legacy boolean flag. Once read using utf-8-sig encoding, diagnostic telemetry is dispatched through utils.output.emit_raw.

Parameters:

  • template_name (str): The base filename of the template without the .md extension (e.g., "extract_facts", "draft_chapters").
  • advanced_mode (bool): Legacy fallback flag indicating whether to load from prompts/advanced/ instead of prompts/tutorial/ when mode is None. Defaults to False.
  • mode (str | None): The explicit operational mode subdirectory name (e.g., "api-reference", "sdk", "common"). Defaults to None.

Returns:

  • str: The decoded content of the prompt template file.

Raises:

  • FileNotFoundError: If the constructed template path does not exist on disk.
  • OSError: If an I/O error occurs while opening or reading the file.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def load_prompt_template(template_name, advanced_mode=False, mode=None):
    if mode is None:
        prompt_dir = "advanced" if advanced_mode else "tutorial"
    else:
        prompt_dir = mode

    path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))), "prompts", prompt_dir, f"{template_name}.md")
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        content = f.read()
    from utils.output import emit_raw

    emit_raw("DEBUG", f"load_prompt_template | loaded '{template_name}.md' from prompts/{prompt_dir}/", dest="LOG")
    return content

The function computes the target directory by resolving mode, defaulting to "advanced" or "tutorial" based on advanced_mode. It constructs an absolute filesystem path relative to the module's parent directory, pointing into prompts/<prompt_dir>/<template_name>.md. The template is loaded with utf-8-sig to automatically strip potential byte-order marks. It then performs a late import of emit_raw from utils.output to record a debug event to the log file before returning the raw template string.

docs.title: parse_yaml_response()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_yaml_response(response):

Description: Parses structured YAML content from an LLM response string enclosed within triple-backtick Markdown blocks (```yaml ... ```). It guards against truncated responses by checking the response's metadata before attempting extraction and parsing via PyYAML.

Parameters:

  • response (str | Any): The text response returned by the LLM, or a specialized string wrapper instance (such as TruncatedResponse).

Returns:

  • Any: The deserialized Python data structure (typically a dictionary or list) resulting from yaml.safe_load().

Raises:

  • ValueError: Raised if the response carries an active truncated = True attribute, if no valid ```yaml fence is found, or if yaml.safe_load() encounters a syntax error.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def parse_yaml_response(response):
    if getattr(response, "truncated", False):
        raise ValueError("LLM response was truncated before the YAML block completed")
    try:
        yaml_str = response.strip().split("```yaml")[1].split("```")[0].strip()
        return yaml.safe_load(yaml_str)
    except Exception as e:
        raise ValueError(f"Failed to parse YAML: {e}") from e

The implementation first inspects the truncated attribute on the incoming response object; if truthy, it immediately aborts parsing with a ValueError so calling nodes can trigger retries rather than processing partial data. It then splits the text across delimiters, isolating the content between the first opening ```yaml fence and the next closing ``` marker. The resulting substring is stripped of whitespace and passed to yaml.safe_load(). Any parsing or delimiter extraction failure is caught and re-raised as a descriptive ValueError.

docs.title: parse_grouping_response()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_grouping_response(response):

Description: Parses the YAML payload generated by the group_modules.md prompt, which defines documentation sidebar sections, descriptive overviews, and inter-module dependencies. If standard YAML parsing fails, the function falls back to a lenient recovery strategy: it strips illegal backticks enclosing section role values and partitions the payload by its primary keys (sections:, descriptions:, dependencies:), parsing each chunk independently.

Parameters:

  • response (str | Any): The raw text response returned by the LLM.

Returns:

  • dict[str, Any]: The parsed dictionary containing the recovered grouping data, guaranteed to include a valid "sections" list.

Raises:

  • ValueError: Raised if the response was truncated, lacks a ```yaml code fence, or if the primary "sections" list cannot be recovered.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def parse_grouping_response(response):
    try:
        return parse_yaml_response(response)
    except ValueError:
        if getattr(response, "truncated", False) or "```yaml" not in response:
            raise
        yaml_str = response.split("```yaml", 1)[1].split("```", 1)[0]
        yaml_str = re.sub(r"(?m)^(\s*(?:-\s+)?role\s*:\s*)`([^`\n]*)`", r"\1\2", yaml_str)
        parsed = {}
        for chunk in re.split(r"(?m)^(?=(?:sections|descriptions|dependencies)\s*:)", yaml_str):
            try:
                part = yaml.safe_load(chunk)
            except Exception:
                continue
            if isinstance(part, dict):
                parsed.update(part)
        if not isinstance(parsed.get("sections"), list):
            raise ValueError("Failed to parse YAML: no sections list in the grouping reply") from None
        return parsed

The function first attempts a strict parse via parse_yaml_response(). If that raises a ValueError, it checks whether the failure was caused by response truncation or a completely missing code block, re-raising immediately if so. Otherwise, it extracts the raw YAML substring and applies a multiline regular expression substitution to remove backticks wrapping role: values, which models often generate when quoting roles. It then splits the text using a positive lookahead regex matching the top-level keys (sections:, descriptions:, dependencies:). Each chunk is individually parsed with yaml.safe_load() and merged into a composite dictionary. If the resulting dictionary does not contain a list under "sections", the function raises a terminal ValueError.

docs.title: build_verified_facts_block()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def build_verified_facts_block(facts: dict | None, doc_paths: dict) -> str:

Description: Constructs the {verified_facts} prompt injection block for api-reference/draft_chapters.md. It formats ground-truth assertions validated by AST analysis—including verified symbols with normalized signatures, imported module dependencies linked to documentation filenames, configuration settings, and raised or defined errors. If facts are absent or extraction failed (claims is None), it returns an empty string.

Parameters:

  • facts (dict | None): A dictionary containing verified file facts conforming to the schema created by utils.facts. Expected keys include "claims", "symbols", "depends_on", "config", and "errors".
  • doc_paths (dict[str, str]): A mapping of repository module paths to their target Markdown chapter documentation filenames (e.g., {"utils/output.py": "utils/output.py.md"}).

Returns:

  • str: A formatted Markdown text block detailing the verified facts, or an empty string if no valid facts exist.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions. Missing dictionary keys default to empty collections.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def build_verified_facts_block(facts: dict | None, doc_paths: dict) -> str:
    if not facts or facts.get("claims") is None:
        return ""
    symbols = facts.get("symbols") or []
    modules = list(dict.fromkeys(edge["module"] for edge in facts.get("depends_on") or []))
    config = facts.get("config") or []
    errors = list(dict.fromkeys(item["name"] for item in facts.get("errors") or [] if item.get("role", "raised") != "caught"))
    if not (symbols or modules or config or errors):
        return ""
    lines = ["VERIFIED FACTS OF THIS FILE (extracted from it and checked against its source code):"]
    if symbols:
        lines.append(
            "Symbols — document every one; copy each signature as written here (one marked 'start of the declaration' continues in the source: copy it in full from there):"
        )
        for symbol in symbols:
            owner = f"{symbol['parent']}." if symbol.get("parent") else ""
            visibility = f", {symbol['visibility']}" if symbol.get("visibility") else ""
            signature, partial = _fact_signature(symbol)
            marker = " — start of the declaration" if partial else ""
            lines.append(
                f"- {symbol.get('kind') or 'symbol'} {owner}{symbol['name']}{visibility} (line {symbol['line']}): {_code_span(signature)}{marker}"
            )
    if modules:
        lines.append("Project files this file imports — See Also must link each of them:")
        lines.extend(f"- {module} (doc: {doc_paths.get(module, module + '.md')})" for module in modules)
    if config:
        lines.append("Configuration it reads: " + ", ".join(f"{item['name']} ({item.get('kind') or 'config'})" for item in config))
    if errors:
        lines.append("Errors it raises or defines: " + ", ".join(errors))
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"

The function checks that facts is present and that facts.get("claims") is not None. It extracts unique module dependencies from depends_on, configuration items from config, and non-caught error types from errors. If no items exist across all categories, it returns an empty string. Otherwise, it compiles a structured bulleted text block. Each symbol is formatted with its parent ownership, visibility modifier, line coordinate, and signature generated by _fact_signature(). Signatures flagged as partial receive an explicit " — start of the declaration" suffix instructing downstream generation steps to extract full signatures from source.

docs.title: build_facts_focus_note()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def build_facts_focus_note(lines: list[tuple[int, str]], limit: int = FACTS_FOCUS_LIMIT) -> str:

Description: Generates the {focus_note} prompt segment for follow-up fact extraction requests using extract_facts.md. When an initial extraction pass overlooks code lines that appear to contain declarations or imports, this function formats those lines up to limit entries, truncating overly long lines to prevent prompt token bloat.

Parameters:

  • lines (list[tuple[int, str]]): A list of tuples where each element contains the 1-based line number and the raw text of an uncovered source code line.
  • limit (int): The maximum number of uncovered lines to render explicitly. Defaults to FACTS_FOCUS_LIMIT (60).

Returns:

  • str: The formatted follow-up instruction string including line-indexed excerpts and an optional count of remaining omitted lines.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def build_facts_focus_note(lines: list[tuple[int, str]], limit: int = FACTS_FOCUS_LIMIT) -> str:
    def shown_line(text: str) -> str:
        text = text.strip()
        return text if len(text) <= _FOCUS_LINE_CHARS else text[: _FOCUS_LINE_CHARS - 3] + "..."

    shown = "\n".join(f"  {number}: {shown_line(text)}" for number, text in lines[:limit])
    more = f"\n  ... and {len(lines) - limit} more such lines" if len(lines) > limit else ""
    return (
        "FOLLOW-UP: a first pass over this file reported nothing for the lines below, which look like declarations "
        "or imports. Report ONLY the facts on these lines, with the same four lists and rules; a line that is not a "
        "declaration a reader looks up (a local variable, a statement) gets nothing.\n"
        f"Lines:\n{shown}{more}\n"
    )

The function defines an internal helper, shown_line(), which strips leading/trailing whitespace and truncates lines exceeding _FOCUS_LINE_CHARS (200 characters), appending an ellipsis (...). It slices the input lines sequence up to limit, formatting each as " {number}: {text}". If the total line count exceeds limit, an overflow string ("... and N more such lines") is appended. The resulting lines are embedded into a standardized instruction block directing the LLM to inspect only the designated line coordinates.

docs.title: parse_facts_response()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_facts_response(response, keys: tuple = FACTS_KEYS) -> dict:

Description: Parses the YAML output of extract_facts.md or extract_manifest.md into a structured dictionary mapping fact categories to item lists. It incorporates a resilient parsing strategy: scalars are kept as raw strings via yaml.BaseLoader, indicator-led values are escaped, and plain-text quotes are converted to block scalars. If full-document parsing fails, it falls back to item-by-item salvage via _salvage_yaml_lists(). Non-dictionary entries and unrecoverable elements are recorded in an "unparsed" count.

Parameters:

  • response (str | Any): The text response returned by the LLM, or a response wrapper.
  • keys (tuple[str, ...]): The collection of expected top-level section keys. Defaults to FACTS_KEYS (("symbols", "dependencies", "config", "errors")).

Returns:

  • dict[str, list[dict] | int]: A dictionary containing the parsed list of mapping objects for each key in keys, alongside an "unparsed" integer key indicating the count of lost or invalid entries.

Raises:

  • ValueError: Raised if the response object has truncated = True, if no opening YAML code block is found, or if none of the target keys can be parsed.

docs.title: Phase 1: Truncation Check and Fence Extraction
docs.text:
# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
    if getattr(response, "truncated", False):
        raise ValueError("LLM response was truncated before the YAML block completed")
    match = _FACTS_BLOCK_RE.search(response) or _FACTS_OPEN_RE.search(response)
    if not match:
        raise ValueError("Failed to parse YAML: no ```yaml block in the facts reply")
    indent = match.group(1)
    yaml_str = _quote_indicator_values("\n".join(line.removeprefix(indent) for line in match.group(2).split("\n")))

The initial phase validates that the generation was not truncated by inspecting the truncated attribute. It then searches for a Markdown code fence using _FACTS_BLOCK_RE (closed block with matching fence indentation) or _FACTS_OPEN_RE (unclosed block). If neither pattern matches, a ValueError is raised. The common indentation captured from the opening fence is stripped from every line of the body, and _quote_indicator_values() sanitizes values starting with YAML indicator tokens.

docs.title: Phase 2: Tiered Parsing and Salvage Execution
docs.text:
# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
    unparsed = 0
    try:
        data = _load_strings(yaml_str)
    except Exception:
        try:
            data = _load_strings(_block_quotes(yaml_str))
        except Exception:
            data, unparsed = _salvage_yaml_lists(_block_quotes(yaml_str), keys)
    if not isinstance(data, dict) or not any(key in data for key in keys):
        raise ValueError("Failed to parse YAML: no fact lists in the facts reply")

The parsing phase attempts deserialization across three progressive tiers. First, it tries parsing the sanitized string directly with _load_strings(). If a syntax error occurs, it rewrites plain scalar signatures and evidence lines into YAML block scalars (|-) via _block_quotes() and retries _load_strings(). If that also fails, it invokes _salvage_yaml_lists(), which decomposes the text by section and recovers list items individually while counting dropped elements. If the recovered data is not a dictionary or contains none of the requested keys, execution terminates with a ValueError.

docs.title: Phase 3: List Filtering and Unparsed Fact Accounting
docs.text:
# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
    result = {}
    for key in keys:
        items = data.get(key)
        items = items if isinstance(items, list) else []
        result[key] = [item for item in items if isinstance(item, dict)]
        unparsed += len(items) - len(result[key])
    result["unparsed"] = unparsed
    return result

In the final phase, each target key is normalized into a list of dictionaries. If a key is missing or set to None, it defaults to an empty list. Any item within a list that is not a dictionary mapping (for example, raw strings or nested arrays generated by formatting errors) is excluded, and its omission increments unparsed. The resulting mapping containing all filtered lists and the final unparsed count is returned.

docs.title: build_code_file_filter_prompt()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def build_code_file_filter_prompt(project_name: str, file_listing: str) -> str:

Description: Constructs the prompt for DeterministicFileMapper in api-reference mode. The prompt instructs the LLM to analyze a project file manifest and categorize files into executable source code modules (containing APIs, classes, or logic) versus project manifest files (such as package.json, Cargo.toml, or pyproject.toml) that define module naming, aliases, or package boundaries.

Parameters:

  • project_name (str): The name of the project or repository being analyzed.
  • file_listing (str): A multi-line string containing the indexed file tree of the target repository.

Returns:

  • str: The fully compiled prompt text requiring a YAML-only response format containing code and manifests index lists.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def build_code_file_filter_prompt(project_name: str, file_listing: str) -> str:
    return (
        f"For the project `{project_name}`, here is the list of all files in the codebase:

"
        f"{file_listing}

"
        f"Your task is to identify WHICH of these files are ACTUAL CODE files that contain "
        f"APIs, functions, classes, or core business logic.
"
        f"EXCLUDE: UI layouts (like .xaml, .storyboard, .html), configuration files "
        f"(like .xml, .json, .manifest, .ini), static assets, build scripts "
        f"(like .csproj, .sln), and documentation.

"
        f"Separately, list the MANIFESTS among the other files: files that declare a package, module, crate or "
        f"workspace name, or import path aliases, for this project's own code (for example package.json, "
        f"tsconfig.json, go.mod, Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, setup.cfg, composer.json, pom.xml, build.gradle, "
        f"*.csproj, mix.exs, pubspec.yaml, *.gemspec).

"
        f"Return ONLY YAML with the file indices of both lists:

"
        f"```yaml
code:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 3
manifests:
  - 2
```"
    )

The function interpolates project_name and file_listing into a pre-defined template string. The template establishes explicit inclusion rules (APIs, business logic) and exclusion boundaries (UI markup, configuration, documentation), while defining package descriptors to classify under the manifests category. It concludes by defining the exact YAML schema expected from the model.

docs.title: build_chapter_summary_prompt()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def build_chapter_summary_prompt(chapter_num: int, abstraction_name: str, chapter_content: str, language: str = "english") -> str:

Description: Constructs a prompt that directs an LLM to generate a concise, four-dimension technical summary of a newly drafted documentation chapter. The resulting brief captures component scope, key technical elements, implementation patterns, and system integration points, which is then injected into subsequent chapter prompts to maintain cross-chapter narrative coherence.

Parameters:

  • chapter_num (int): The 1-based sequential number of the completed chapter.
  • abstraction_name (str): The name of the abstraction or module documented in the chapter.
  • chapter_content (str): The full Markdown text of the generated chapter.
  • language (str): The target language for the summary output. Defaults to "english".

Returns:

  • str: The formatted summary prompt including structural requirements and chapter text.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def build_chapter_summary_prompt(chapter_num: int, abstraction_name: str, chapter_content: str, language: str = "english") -> str:
    lang_instruction = f"Write the entire summary in {language.capitalize()}. " if language.lower() != "english" else ""
    return (
        f"{lang_instruction}"
        f"Summarize the following documentation chapter as a structured technical brief. "
        f"For EACH of the 4 points below, write 3-5 concise technical sentences:\n\n"
        f"(1) **Component Scope & Responsibility**: What is the main technical domain this "
        f"chapter covers? What problems does it solve and what role does it play in the system?\n\n"
        f"(2) **Key Technical Elements**: What are the specific classes, services, functions, "
        f"data models, or protocols discussed? Name them and describe their concrete roles.\n\n"
        f"(3) **Implementation Patterns & Architecture**: What design patterns, communication "
        f"protocols, data flow strategies, error handling mechanisms, or security measures "
        f"are covered? How are they implemented?\n\n"
        f"(4) **System Integration & Dependencies**: How does this component interface with "
        f"other parts of the system? What does it consume from or provide to other components? "
        f"What are the key integration points?\n\n"
        f"---\n"
        f"Chapter {chapter_num}: {abstraction_name}\n"
        f"{chapter_content}"
    )

The function evaluates the language argument and conditionally prepends a localization directive when the target language is not English. It formats four technical dimensions requiring 3 to 5 sentences each to balance technical detail with token economy. The target chapter number, abstraction name, and chapter body are appended after a separator line.

docs.title: _INDEX_RE
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _INDEX_RE = re.compile(r"^\s*(\d+)\s*(?:#.*)?$")

Description: Regular expression compiled to match a single integer file index optionally surrounded by whitespace and followed by an inline comment starting with #.

docs.title: _INDEX_RANGE_RE
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _INDEX_RANGE_RE = re.compile(r"^\s*(\d+)\s*(?:-|\.\.|\u2013|to)\s*(\d+)\s*(?:#.*)?$")

Description: Regular expression compiled to match ascending integer ranges delimited by hyphens (-), double dots (..), en-dashes (\u2013), or the word to, with optional trailing comment annotations.

docs.title: _FACTS_BLOCK_RE
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _FACTS_BLOCK_RE = re.compile(r"(?msi)^([ \t]*)```ya?ml[^\n]*\n(.*?)^\1```[ \t]*$")

Description: Multiline, dot-all, case-insensitive regular expression matching a closed YAML Markdown code fence. It captures leading indentation on the opening fence and requires the closing fence to match that exact indentation, preventing nested triple-backtick docstrings inside block scalars from terminating the block prematurely.

docs.title: _FACTS_OPEN_RE
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _FACTS_OPEN_RE = re.compile(r"(?msi)^([ \t]*)```ya?ml[^\n]*\n(.*)")

Description: Regular expression matching an unclosed YAML code fence. Used as a fallback when the LLM omits the closing triple backticks or the response ends abruptly.

docs.title: _PLAIN_QUOTE_RE
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _PLAIN_QUOTE_RE = re.compile(r"(?m)^([ \t]*(?:- )?)(signature|evidence):[ \t]+(\S.*)$")

Description: Matches unquoted signature: or evidence: key-value lines that contain colons or comment markers that would break standard YAML parsing.

docs.title: _WHOLE_SCALAR_RE
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _WHOLE_SCALAR_RE = re.compile(r"""^(?:"(?:\\.|[^"\\])*"|'(?:''|[^'])*'|[|>][-+0-9]*)[ \t]*(?:#.*)?$""")

Description: Identifies scalar values that are already properly enclosed in double quotes, single quotes, or YAML block scalar indicators (|, >), ensuring valid entries are not re-processed.

docs.title: _INDICATOR_VALUE_RE
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _INDICATOR_VALUE_RE = re.compile(r"(?m)^([ \t]*(?:- )?(?:name|entry|alias|target|base|parent):[ \t]+)([@#&!%]\S||>\S)(?:[ \t]+#.)?$")`

Description: Matches YAML mapping values for specific identifier keys (name, entry, alias, target, base, parent) that begin with prohibited YAML indicators (such as @, #, *, &, or backticks) that would otherwise cause syntax errors.

docs.title: _FACT_SIGNATURE_CHARS
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _FACT_SIGNATURE_CHARS = 200

Description: Character limit threshold for symbol signatures rendered in verified facts blocks. Signatures exceeding this length are truncated with an ellipsis and flagged as partial declarations.

docs.title: _FOCUS_LINE_CHARS
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _FOCUS_LINE_CHARS = 200

Description: Character threshold for lines displayed in follow-up fact focus notes. Lines exceeding this limit are truncated to conserve prompt context tokens.

docs.title: _fact_signature()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _fact_signature(symbol: dict) -> tuple[str, bool]:

Description: Formats and normalizes a verified symbol signature for prompt injection. It strips leading decorators or language-specific attributes, collapses multiline whitespace into a single line, removes string literals to check bracket balance, and detects truncation.

Parameters:

  • symbol (dict): The symbol dictionary extracted by static analysis, containing keys like "signature" and "truncated".

Returns:

  • tuple[str, bool]: A 2-tuple containing the sanitized signature string and a boolean flag indicating whether the signature is incomplete (True) or complete (False).

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def _fact_signature(symbol: dict) -> tuple[str, bool]:
    lines = str(symbol.get("signature", "")).split("\n")
    while len(lines) > 1 and re.match(r"\s*(?:@|#\[|\[[A-Z])", lines[0]):  # @property, #[inline], [Obsolete]
        lines = lines[1:]
    text = " ".join(" ".join(lines).split())
    code = re.sub(r"\"(?:\\.|[^\"\\])*\"|'(?:\\.|[^'\\])*'", "", text)
    partial = bool(symbol.get("truncated")) or code.count("(") > code.count(")") or code.count("[") > code.count("]")
    if len(text) > _FACT_SIGNATURE_CHARS:
        text, partial = text[:_FACT_SIGNATURE_CHARS].rstrip(), True
    return (text + " …" if partial else text), partial

The function splits the signature on newlines and drops leading decorator and attribute lines matching patterns like @property, #[inline], or [Obsolete]. It collapses all remaining whitespace runs into single spaces. To test whether the signature was cut short, it strips string literals and checks for unbalanced opening parentheses or square brackets. If the signature is marked truncated, has unbalanced brackets, or exceeds _FACT_SIGNATURE_CHARS (200 characters), partial is set to True, and the signature text is truncated with a trailing " …".

docs.title: _code_span()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _code_span(text: str) -> str:

Description: Wraps an arbitrary text string inside an inline Markdown code span using a backtick sequence long enough that backticks within the text cannot prematurely close the fence.

Parameters:

  • text (str): The raw text to wrap as an inline code snippet.

Returns:

  • str: The fenced inline code span string.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def _code_span(text: str) -> str:
    fence = "`" * (max((len(run) for run in re.findall(r"`+", text)), default=0) + 1)
    return f"{fence} {text} {fence}" if "`" in text else f"{fence}{text}{fence}"

The function scans the input string for all contiguous sequences of backtick characters (+) and determines the maximum length among them. It constructs an outer delimiter fence with a length equal to that maximum plus one. If the enclosed text contains backticks, spaces are added inside the delimiters according to CommonMark inline code rules; otherwise, the fence sits flush against the text.

docs.title: _load_strings()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _load_strings(text: str):

Description: Deserializes a YAML string using yaml.BaseLoader so that all scalar values (such as HTTP status codes 404, boolean-like words on/off, and version strings 3.10) remain plain Python strings rather than being coerced into numbers or booleans.

Parameters:

  • text (str): The raw YAML string to load.

Returns:

  • Any: The deserialized Python data structure consisting exclusively of str, list, and dict types.

Raises:

  • yaml.YAMLError: If the string cannot be parsed as valid YAML under yaml.BaseLoader.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def _load_strings(text: str):
    return yaml.load(text, Loader=yaml.BaseLoader)  # BaseLoader builds only str / list / dict: safe

The helper delegates directly to yaml.load(text, Loader=yaml.BaseLoader). Using BaseLoader avoids PyYAML's automatic type casting rules (where unquoted yes, no, true, 3.10, or 123 are converted to booleans and numbers), preserving the exact string tokens emitted by the LLM for downstream code matching.

docs.title: _quote_indicator_values()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _quote_indicator_values(text: str) -> str:

Description: Scans a YAML string and encloses problematic scalar values starting with special indicator tokens in double quotes, escaping any backslashes or internal quotes.

Parameters:

  • text (str): The raw YAML string.

Returns:

  • str: The sanitized YAML string with problematic scalar values safely double-quoted.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def _quote_indicator_values(text: str) -> str:
    return _INDICATOR_VALUE_RE.sub(lambda m: m[1] + '"' + m[2].replace("\\", "\\\\").replace('"', '\\"') + '"', text)

The helper uses _INDICATOR_VALUE_RE to locate target mapping keys whose scalar values begin with characters like @, #, *, or &. A lambda substitution escapes backslashes and double quotes within the matched value, wrapping the result in double quotes while preserving leading key indentation.

docs.title: _block_quotes()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _block_quotes(text: str) -> str:

Description: Converts unquoted signature: or evidence: mapping entries into YAML block scalars (|-), preventing unescaped colons, hashes, or quotes from causing syntax errors.

Parameters:

  • text (str): The raw YAML text to transform.

Returns:

  • str: The modified YAML text with unquoted scalar values rewritten into indented block scalar blocks.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
def _block_quotes(text: str) -> str:
    return _PLAIN_QUOTE_RE.sub(lambda m: m[0] if _WHOLE_SCALAR_RE.match(m[3]) else f"{m[1]}{m[2]}: |-\n{' ' * (len(m[1]) + 2)}{m[3]}", text)

The function executes a regex substitution using _PLAIN_QUOTE_RE. For each matched signature: or evidence: entry, it checks whether the value already forms a valid scalar via _WHOLE_SCALAR_RE. If it does, the line is left untouched. Otherwise, it rewrites the line using a strip-chomped block scalar indicator (|-), placing the original value on the next line with two additional spaces of indentation.

docs.title: _salvage_yaml_lists()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _salvage_yaml_lists(yaml_str: str, keys: tuple) -> tuple[dict, int]:

Description: A fallback parser for malformed YAML responses. It partitions the YAML text into top-level key sections; if a section fails to parse as a whole, it splits that section into individual list items based on bullet indentation (-), parsing each item independently. Successfully parsed mapping items are retained, while corrupt items are counted as lost.

Parameters:

  • yaml_str (str): The sanitized YAML text that failed whole-document parsing.
  • keys (tuple[str, ...]): The tuple of expected top-level key names to extract.

Returns:

  • tuple[dict[str, list[dict]], int]: A 2-tuple where the first element is the recovered dictionary mapping section keys to lists of parsed dictionaries, and the second element is an integer count of list items that could not be parsed.

docs.title: Phase 1: Top-Level Section Partitioning
docs.text:
# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
    names = "|".join(keys)
    parsed, lost = {}, 0
    for chunk in re.split(rf"(?m)^(?=(?:{names})\s*:)", yaml_str):
        head = re.match(rf"({names})\s*:", chunk)
        if not head:
            continue
        try:
            part = _load_strings(chunk)
        except Exception:
            part = None
        if isinstance(part, dict):
            parsed.update(part)
            continue

The function builds an alternation pattern of the target keys and splits yaml_str at lines beginning with any of those section headers. For each identified chunk, it extracts the matching key name. It first attempts to parse the entire chunk with _load_strings(). If successful and the result is a dictionary, the chunk is merged into parsed and the loop advances to the next section.

docs.title: Phase 2: Granular Item-by-Item Salvage
docs.text:
# Extracted from utils/prompts.py
        body = chunk[head.end() :]
        first = re.search(r"(?m)^([ \t]*)- ", body)
        if not first:
            continue
        indent = first.group(1)
        items = []
        for piece in re.split(rf"(?m)^(?={re.escape(indent)}- )", body):
            if not piece.startswith(f"{indent}- "):
                continue
            text = "\n".join(line.removeprefix(indent) for line in piece.split("\n"))
            try:
                item = _load_strings(text)
            except Exception:
                lost += 1
                continue
            if isinstance(item, list) and item and isinstance(item[0], dict):
                items.append(item[0])
            else:
                lost += 1
        parsed[head.group(1)] = items
    return parsed, lost

If the entire section chunk fails to parse, the helper strips the header line and locates the indentation of the first bullet list item (-). Using that indentation level, it splits the section body into individual item fragments. For each fragment, it removes the common bullet indentation and attempts to parse it via _load_strings(). If an item fails to parse or resolves to something other than a single-item list containing a dictionary, the lost counter increments. Valid dictionary items are appended to items, and the section key is updated with the recovered items before returning the (parsed, lost) tuple.

docs.title: Facts extraction result dictionary
docs.text:
Returned by parse_facts_response(), representing parsed codebase facts extracted from an LLM response alongside a count of lost items.

Field Type Description symbols list[dict] Verified symbol declarations (classes, functions, methods, constants). dependencies list[dict] Imported file paths, external modules, and package dependencies. config list[dict] Environment variables, configuration settings, or flags read by the file. errors list[dict] Exception classes, custom errors, and error types raised or defined. unparsed int Count of list items that were dropped due to syntax errors or non-mapping types.

Example dictionary structure:

{
    "symbols": [
        {"name": "load_prompt_template", "line": 55, "kind": "function"}
    ],
    "dependencies": [
        {"module": "utils/output.py"}
    ],
    "config": [],
    "errors": [
        {"name": "ValueError", "role": "raised"}
    ],
    "unparsed": 0
}

docs.title: Module grouping response dictionary
docs.text:
Returned by parse_grouping_response(), containing the documentation sidebar structure and inter-module dependencies.

Field Type Description sections list[dict] Hierarchical documentation section definitions with titles and included file paths. descriptions dict[str, str] Markdown overviews describing the responsibilities of each logical section. dependencies list[dict] Structural relationships and cross-section import links between modules.

Example dictionary structure:

{
    "sections": [
        {
            "title": "Utilities",
            "files": ["utils/output.py", "utils/prompts.py"]
        }
    ],
    "descriptions": {
        "Utilities": "Core logging, configuration, and prompt helper modules."
    },
    "dependencies": []
}

docs.title: Verified facts input dictionary
docs.text:
The schema of the facts dictionary passed to build_verified_facts_block(), representing facts verified against source code by utils.facts.

Field Type Description claims Any | None Status indicator for claim verification; if None, the file is treated as having no verified facts. symbols list[dict] Symbol metadata dictionaries containing name, line, signature, and optional parent and visibility. depends_on list[dict] Dependency edges containing at minimum a module string identifying an imported target. config list[dict] Configuration entries containing name and optional kind. errors list[dict] Error descriptors containing name and role ("raised", "defined", or "caught").

Example dictionary structure:

{
    "claims": True,
    "symbols": [
        {
            "name": "parse_file_index",
            "parent": None,
            "visibility": "public",
            "line": 16,
            "signature": "def parse_file_index(idx_value):",
            "truncated": False
        }
    ],
    "depends_on": [
        {"module": "utils/output.py"}
    ],
    "config": [],
    "errors": [
        {"name": "ValueError", "role": "raised"}
    ]
}

docs.title: Salvaged YAML lists tuple
docs.text:
Returned by internal helper _salvage_yaml_lists(), pairing recovered section lists with a count of lost items.

Index Type Description 0 dict[str, list[dict]] Dictionary mapping top-level section keys to lists of successfully parsed dictionary items. 1 int Count of list items that failed to parse or did not contain valid mapping structures.

docs.title: Fact signature metadata tuple
docs.text:
Returned by internal helper _fact_signature(), describing a processed symbol signature.

Index Type Description 0 str Normalized, single-line signature text, truncated with an ellipsis if incomplete. 1 bool Incompletion flag: True if truncated, bracket-unbalanced, or exceeding 200 characters; False otherwise.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
utils/prompts.py enforces explicit error-handling strategies to balance data integrity with fault tolerance during LLM inference:

  • Truncation Detection: Functions that parse LLM output (parse_yaml_response(), parse_grouping_response(), and parse_facts_response()) inspect incoming response objects for an active truncated = True attribute (typically set on TruncatedResponse instances from llm_common). When detected, they immediately raise a ValueError rather than parsing incomplete YAML that might silently drop symbols, dependencies, or chapters.
  • Progressive Parsing Fallback: When structured YAML syntax errors occur, parse_facts_response() applies a multi-tiered recovery process rather than failing immediately. It runs regex transformations to quote unquoted indicators, converts plain scalar quotes into block scalars, and partitions corrupted sections down to individual list items via _salvage_yaml_lists().
  • Unparsed Fact Accounting: Dropped, unparseable, or non-mapping items encountered during YAML salvage do not abort execution; instead, they increment an explicit "unparsed" integer counter returned to the caller. This allows downstream quality-assurance systems (such as chapter_check.py) to account for claimed-but-unverified assertions.
  • Lenient Recovery with Fail-Fast Validation: In parse_grouping_response(), syntax recovery is attempted by unwrapping backtick-enclosed roles and splitting the input across known top-level keys. However, if the recovered payload still lacks a valid "sections" list, it raises a ValueError to ensure downstream site generators do not receive invalid navigation structures.

docs.title: thinking.py
docs.text: Source: utils/thinking.py

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
The utils/thinking.py module establishes the centralized reasoning effort resolution engine—termed "thinking flows"—for the Codebase-Knowledge-Builder pipeline. Across contemporary reasoning models (including Anthropic Claude 3.7/Opus, Google Gemini 2.5/3.x, and various OpenRouter models), explicit thinking parameters serve as the primary lever balancing token expenditure against synthesis quality. Rather than hardcoding reasoning levels inside disparate generation steps, this module assigns a unique node key to every Large Language Model (LLM) interaction point and resolves an execution-wide dictionary mapping each node to a calibrated effort level.

The module manages configuration precedence across CLI flags, provider capabilities, and execution modes. When orchestrating pipeline initialization, it resolves profile settings (--thinking-profile), global overrides (--thinking-level), and surgical per-node overrides (--thinking-override NODE=LEVEL). For providers that support fine-grained thinking controls (ANTHROPIC, GEMINI, and OPENROUTER), the default auto profile activates a balanced tier (balanced), whereas unmapped providers (such as local Ollama or OpenAI-compatible proxies) default to disabled thinking (off). Furthermore, the module handles operational mode nuances—such as boosting chapter writing effort in advanced mode to accommodate architectural design rationale—and provides nearest-neighbor clamping routines to reconcile abstract effort requests with discrete provider limits.

docs.title: THINKING_LEVELS
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: THINKING_LEVELS = ("minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max")

Description: An ordered tuple defining the project's canonical effort scale. Represents an increasing gradient of token expenditure and reasoning depth. The minimal level exists primarily for models exposed via OpenRouter that support an ultra-low reasoning boundary, though standard built-in profiles operate within the low to max spectrum.

THINKING_LEVELS = ("minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max")

The THINKING_LEVELS constant acts as the standard reference scale across all pipeline modules. It provides the index coordinates used by clamp_level when calculating relative distances between requested levels and provider-supported feature sets. Because it is ordered strictly from lowest to highest effort, index differences directly reflect relative reasoning distance.

docs.title: THINKING_PROFILES
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: THINKING_PROFILES = ("auto", "off", "economy", "balanced", "quality", "max")

Description: An immutable tuple enumerating the valid configuration profile names accepted from CLI parameters or environment flags.

THINKING_PROFILES = ("auto", "off", "economy", "balanced", "quality", "max")

This tuple defines the allowed user options for the --thinking-profile flag. The entries correspond to curated strategies: auto dynamically evaluates the provider; off suppresses thinking parameters; economy minimizes tokens across mechanical steps; balanced provides standard production trade-offs; quality elevates reasoning across synthesis phases; and max allocates the highest supported effort across all analytical nodes.

docs.title: NODE_KEYS
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: NODE_KEYS = ( "filter_files", "extract_facts", "map_abstractions", "reduce_abstractions", "identify_abstractions", "analyze_relationships", "order_chapters", "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "group_modules", "translate_strings" )

Description: A comprehensive tuple registering all LLM call sites within the execution pipeline in approximate chronological order.

NODE_KEYS = (
    "filter_files",  # DeterministicFileMapper — code/non-code file classification (api-reference)
    "extract_facts",  # ExtractFacts — per-file symbols, dependencies, config, errors with source quotes (api-reference)
    "map_abstractions",  # MapAbstractions — per-batch abstraction extraction (batch route)
    "reduce_abstractions",  # ReduceAbstractions — merge partial abstractions (batch route)
    "identify_abstractions",  # IdentifyAbstractions — whole-codebase abstraction discovery (direct route)
    "analyze_relationships",  # AnalyzeRelationships — project summary + abstraction relationships
    "order_chapters",  # OrderChapters — pedagogical chapter ordering
    "write_chapters",  # WriteChapters — long-form chapter / reference page generation
    "chapter_summary",  # WriteChapters — 3-5 sentence summary for cross-chapter context
    "group_modules",  # CombineTutorial — MkDocs nav grouping (api-reference, 6+ modules)
    "translate_strings",  # i18n — CLI string table translation (first run in a new language)
)

NODE_KEYS functions as the formal schema for pipeline call sites. Each entry matches the step context tag used by PocketFlow pipeline nodes and telemetry loggers. It guarantees that CLI override parsers and profile mappings strictly reference valid, active LLM execution points.

docs.title: MODE_NODES
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: MODE_NODES = { "tutorial": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"), "advanced": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"), "sdk": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"), "api-reference": ("filter_files", "extract_facts", "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "group_modules", "translate_strings"), }

Description: A dictionary mapping pipeline operational modes (tutorial, advanced, sdk, api-reference) to the specific sequence of node keys that execute LLM inferences during that mode.

MODE_NODES = {
    "tutorial": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"),
    "advanced": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"),
    "sdk": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"),
    "api-reference": ("filter_files", "extract_facts", "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "group_modules", "translate_strings"),
}

This mapping reflects the bifurcation between narrative modes and reference modes. While tutorial, advanced, and sdk run the full conceptual analysis sequence defined in _ANALYSIS_NODES, the api-reference mode bypasses speculative abstraction steps, using filter_files and extract_facts for deterministic 1:1 file extraction and introducing group_modules for navigation tree synthesis.

docs.title: PROFILED_PROVIDERS
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: PROFILED_PROVIDERS = ("ANTHROPIC", "GEMINI", "OPENROUTER")

Description: A tuple containing the uppercase identifiers of model providers whose SDKs or APIs support granular reasoning effort levels.

PROFILED_PROVIDERS = ("ANTHROPIC", "GEMINI", "OPENROUTER")

This tuple is evaluated during preflight configuration resolution. When a user runs with --thinking-profile auto, providers in this set activate the balanced profile, whereas providers not in this list fall back to off to prevent sending unsupported reasoning parameters to incompatible API endpoints.

docs.title: resolve_profile_name()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def resolve_profile_name(profile: str | None, provider: str | None) -> str:

Description: Resolves the dynamic auto profile keyword into a concrete profile name based on provider capabilities, while passing through explicit profile names unchanged.

Parameters:

  • profile (str | None): The requested profile name (e.g., from CLI args). Defaults to "auto" if empty or None.
  • provider (str | None): The normalized uppercase model provider name (e.g., "ANTHROPIC", "GEMINI").

Returns:

  • str: The resolved profile name ("balanced", "off", "economy", "quality", or "max").

Raises:

  • None: This function does not explicitly raise any exceptions.

Example:

def resolve_profile_name(profile: str | None, provider: str | None) -> str:
    """Resolve `auto` to a concrete profile for the active provider."""
    profile = (profile or "auto").lower()
    if profile == "auto":
        return "balanced" if provider in PROFILED_PROVIDERS else "off"
    return profile

The function normalizes inputs by lowercasing the profile string and defaulting absent configurations to "auto". For "auto", it queries PROFILED_PROVIDERS; if the active provider supports explicit per-model thinking, it resolves to "balanced". If the provider does not support fine-grained controls, it returns "off". Any explicit profile passed by the caller is returned directly.

docs.title: clamp_level()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def clamp_level(level: str, supported) -> str | None:

Description: Evaluates a requested thinking level against an iterable of supported levels exposed by a model or provider. Returns the level directly if supported, or computes the nearest neighbor along the THINKING_LEVELS scale, resolving distance ties in favor of the lower level.

Parameters:

  • level (str): The requested abstract thinking level.
  • supported (iterable of str): A collection, set, or sequence of levels supported by the target model or driver.

Returns:

  • str | None: The exact or nearest supported level, or None if the input level is not in THINKING_LEVELS or no supported levels match the scale.

Raises:

  • None: This function does not explicitly raise any exceptions.

Example:

def clamp_level(level: str, supported) -> str | None:
    """Return `level` if the model supports it, else the nearest supported level on
    THINKING_LEVELS (ties → lower). None when nothing on the scale is supported."""
    if level in supported:
        return level
    ranked = [lvl for lvl in THINKING_LEVELS if lvl in supported]
    if not ranked or level not in THINKING_LEVELS:
        return None
    target = THINKING_LEVELS.index(level)
    return min(ranked, key=lambda lvl: (abs(THINKING_LEVELS.index(lvl) - target), THINKING_LEVELS.index(lvl)))

This clamping algorithm prevents generation crashes when models expose constrained reasoning tiers (for example, models supporting only low and high). It filters THINKING_LEVELS to find all candidates present in supported. If the target is absent, it computes a composite sort key (distance, index). The second tuple element ensures that if a level is equidistant between two supported levels, the lower-indexed (less expensive) level is selected.

docs.title: parse_overrides()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_overrides(values: list[str] | None) -> tuple[dict, list[str]]:

Description: Parses and validates raw NODE=LEVEL CLI override expressions into a dictionary of valid overrides and a list of malformed or unrecognized expressions.

Parameters:

  • values (list[str] | None): A list of raw string arguments passed via --thinking-override.

Returns:

  • tuple[dict, list[str]]: A 2-tuple containing:
    • overrides (dict[str, str]): Mapping of valid node keys to their overridden thinking levels.
    • invalid (list[str]): List of input strings that failed delimiter, node key, or thinking level validation.

Raises:

  • None: This function does not explicitly raise any exceptions.

Example:

def parse_overrides(values: list[str] | None) -> tuple[dict, list[str]]:
    """Parse NODE=LEVEL strings. Returns (overrides, invalid_values)."""
    overrides, invalid = {}, []
    for value in values or []:
        node, sep, level = value.partition("=")
        node, level = node.strip().lower(), level.strip().lower()
        if not sep or node not in NODE_KEYS or level not in THINKING_LEVELS:
            invalid.append(value)
        else:
            overrides[node] = level
    return overrides, invalid

The function iterates over the input strings, partitioning each on the = delimiter. It sanitizes both tokens by stripping whitespace and converting to lowercase. An item is categorized as invalid if the delimiter is missing, if the node key does not exist in NODE_KEYS, or if the requested level is absent from THINKING_LEVELS. Valid pairs are collected into overrides, and unrecognized entries are retained in invalid for diagnostic logging.

docs.title: build_thinking_plan()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def build_thinking_plan(profile: str, mode: str, global_level: str | None, overrides: dict) -> dict:

Description: Assembles the complete thinking plan dictionary mapping every registered NODE_KEYS item to an effort level or None. Enforces hierarchical precedence across global levels, profile tables, mode adjustments, and per-node overrides.

Parameters:

  • profile (str): The resolved profile name (must not be "auto").
  • mode (str): The active pipeline execution mode ("tutorial", "advanced", "sdk", or "api-reference").
  • global_level (str | None): Global thinking level override (--thinking-level), if specified.
  • overrides (dict): Per-node override mapping produced by parse_overrides().

Returns:

  • dict: A dictionary mapping every node key in NODE_KEYS to a thinking level string or None.

Raises:

  • None: This function does not explicitly raise any exceptions.

Example:

def build_thinking_plan(profile: str, mode: str, global_level: str | None, overrides: dict) -> dict:
    """Return {node_key: level | None} for every NODE key.

    Precedence: overrides > global_level > profile table (+ mode adjustments).
    `profile` must already be resolved (see resolve_profile_name).
    """
    if global_level:
        plan = dict.fromkeys(NODE_KEYS, global_level.lower())
    elif profile in _PROFILES:
        plan = dict(_PROFILES[profile])
        plan.update(_MODE_ADJUSTMENTS.get(profile, {}).get(mode, {}))
    else:  # "off": every node uses the model's default thinking behavior
        plan = dict.fromkeys(NODE_KEYS)
    plan.update(overrides)
    return plan

The construction follows a strict hierarchy. If global_level is provided, every node key is initialized to that uniform level. Otherwise, if the profile exists in _PROFILES, the plan loads the baseline node allocations and applies any mode-specific delta from _MODE_ADJUSTMENTS. If the profile is "off" or unrecognized, all nodes are initialized to None (instructing models to use native defaults). Finally, any explicit per-node entries in overrides overwrite existing values, ensuring surgical overrides take absolute precedence.

docs.title: resolve_thinking_level()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def resolve_thinking_level(shared: dict, node_key: str) -> str | None:

Description: Retrieves the configured thinking effort level for an active pipeline node from the shared execution dictionary.

Parameters:

  • shared (dict): The global or workflow-level shared state dictionary.
  • node_key (str): The identifier of the calling node (from NODE_KEYS).

Returns:

  • str | None: The resolved effort level for the node, or None if unconfigured or disabled.

Raises:

  • None: This function does not explicitly raise any exceptions.

Example:

def resolve_thinking_level(shared: dict, node_key: str) -> str | None:
    """Thinking level for one LLM call site. Falls back to the global level when no plan exists."""
    plan = shared.get("thinking_plan")
    if plan and node_key in plan:
        return plan[node_key]
    return shared.get("thinking_level")

This helper abstracts plan lookup for individual pipeline nodes. It inspects the thinking_plan mapping stored within shared. If a plan is present and contains the target node_key, it returns the assigned level. If no plan is found or the key is omitted, it falls back to the top-level thinking_level attribute in shared, returning None if no reasoning configuration exists.

docs.title: describe_plan()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def describe_plan(plan: dict, mode: str | None = None) -> str:

Description: Formats an active thinking plan into a compact, comma-separated key-value string suitable for startup console emissions and diagnostic logs, filtering output to include only nodes relevant to the current mode.

Parameters:

  • plan (dict): The thinking plan dictionary mapping node keys to levels.
  • mode (str | None): The active execution mode used to filter displayed nodes via MODE_NODES. Defaults to displaying all NODE_KEYS if None or omitted.

Returns:

  • str: A formatted string such as "filter_files=low, extract_facts=low, write_chapters=medium".

Raises:

  • None: This function does not explicitly raise any exceptions.

Example:

def describe_plan(plan: dict, mode: str | None = None) -> str:
    """Compact one-line rendering for the startup config display (only nodes that run in `mode`)."""
    keys = MODE_NODES.get(mode, NODE_KEYS)
    return ", ".join(f"{key}={plan.get(key) or 'default'}" for key in keys)

The function identifies the relevant nodes by querying MODE_NODES with the provided mode, falling back to NODE_KEYS when mode is unlisted or unspecified. It then iterates over those keys, formatting each as key=level. If a node's level is None, it substitutes the label 'default' to indicate that the model's native reasoning behavior applies.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
The module implements defensive parsing and fail-safe validation strategies to prevent configuration errors from halting pipeline execution:

  • Non-Crashing Override Accumulation: In parse_overrides(), malformed CLI strings (such as missing = delimiters, unknown node keys, or unsupported levels) do not raise exceptions. Instead, they are collected into an invalid list and returned to the caller, allowing main.py to log descriptive warnings while applying all valid overrides.
  • Safe Nearest-Neighbor Clamping: The clamp_level() function gracefully handles model constraints without raising errors. If an unsupported thinking level is requested, it calculates relative index distances against THINKING_LEVELS and falls back to the nearest supported level. If the target level is completely unrecognized or the model supports no levels on the scale, it safely returns None.
  • Safe State Lookup: Functions querying state dictionaries (resolve_thinking_level, build_thinking_plan, and describe_plan) use .get() with explicit defaults. Missing keys or uninitialized plans fall back to None or 'default', ensuring execution continues using the model's native settings.
  • String Normalization: All user-supplied strings (profile names, node keys, and effort levels) are sanitized via .strip().lower() before comparison, preventing failures caused by inconsistent casing or whitespace in environment variables and CLI flags.

docs.title: token_utils.py
docs.text: Source: utils/token_utils.py

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
The utils/token_utils.py module serves as the centralized token estimation, context headroom budgeting, and dynamic ratio calibration engine for the Codebase Knowledge Builder pipeline. Foundation models from disparate providers (such as Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, and OpenRouter-hosted models) utilize proprietary Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) or SentencePiece tokenizers with distinct vocabularies. Because downloading and executing vendor-specific tokenizers locally introduces operational overhead and dependency instability, this module adopts OpenAI's cl100k_base encoding (via tiktoken) as a universal baseline and bridges discrepancies through empirical token ratio calibration.

To reconcile the baseline cl100k_base counts with actual provider tokenization, the module implements an asymmetric, sample-weighted online calibration loop. It initializes each model with a static ratio prior resolved from utils.llm_config. As pipeline steps complete LLM requests, observe_prompt_tokens compares the locally measured raw tokens against the provider's billed usage. The calibration system adjusts the effective ratio upwards aggressively to avoid context overflow errors, while lowering it conservatively only when backed by substantial empirical sample sizes and token volumes. These calibrated multipliers are persisted atomically across runs in llm_token_calibration.json.

Beyond ratio estimation, the module calculates prompt sizing boundaries via input_token_budget. It guarantees that prompt payloads leave sufficient headroom for planned model output generations, thinking/reasoning token allocations, fixed provider margins, and dynamic estimation error reserves (scaling from 5% down to 2% once calibrated). High-throughput raw token counting is accelerated via a thread-safe, bounded Least Recently Used (LRU) content cache indexed by text length and Python string object hashes, alongside parallelized multi-threaded batch tokenization for large document arrays.

docs.title: resolve_max_tokens()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def resolve_max_tokens(shared):

Description: Determines the maximum context window capacity available for execution. It inspects the caller-provided shared pipeline state dictionary for an explicit "max_tokens" override; if absent, it queries utils.llm_config.resolve_llm_settings() and utils.llm_config.get_model_context_length() to detect the active provider's native context limit dynamically.

Parameters:

  • shared (dict): The shared execution store containing pipeline state, optionally carrying a pre-configured "max_tokens" integer key.

Returns:

  • int: The resolved context window token capacity.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions directly; network or configuration errors from resolve_llm_settings() or get_model_context_length() may bubble up.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/token_utils.py:47-55
def resolve_max_tokens(shared):
    """Resolve max_tokens from shared store or auto-detect from the active provider."""
    max_tokens = shared.get("max_tokens")
    if max_tokens is not None:
        return max_tokens
    _, model_name, endpoint, api_key = resolve_llm_settings()
    max_tokens_val = get_model_context_length(endpoint, model_name, api_key)
    emit_raw("DEBUG", f"resolve_max_tokens | resolved max_tokens={max_tokens_val:,}", dest="LOG")
    return max_tokens_val

The function checks the shared dictionary before querying external provider settings. When falling back to active configuration inspection, it queries the endpoint and API key to establish context boundaries, logging the resolved value to the diagnostic file stream before returning.

docs.title: input_token_budget()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def input_token_budget(max_tokens: int, thinking_level: str | None = None) -> int:

Description: Computes the maximum safe prompt size (in calibrated token units) that fits within the given context window while guaranteeing adequate headroom for model responses, reasoning tokens, and estimation variance.

docs.title: Phase 1: Output Reserve and Margin Allocation
docs.text:
planned = context_output_reserve(thinking_level)
    if planned is not None:
        reserve = planned + CONTEXT_MARGIN
    else:
        reserve = min(max(int(max_tokens * 0.05), MIN_OUTPUT_RESERVE), MAX_OUTPUT_RESERVE)

The function queries context_output_reserve to determine the token budget required by the provider for the specified thinking tier, appending the static CONTEXT_MARGIN. For providers without explicit output sizing schemas, it reserves 5% of max_tokens, clamping the allocation between MIN_OUTPUT_RESERVE (8,192 tokens) and MAX_OUTPUT_RESERVE (64,000 tokens).

docs.title: Phase 2: Dynamic Estimation Reserve Allocation and Floor Enforcement
docs.text:
reserve += int(max_tokens * (ESTIMATE_RESERVE_CALIBRATED if ratio_is_calibrated() else ESTIMATE_RESERVE_UNCALIBRATED))
    return max(max_tokens - reserve, max_tokens // 2)

The total reserve is expanded by an estimation error factor: 2% (ESTIMATE_RESERVE_CALIBRATED) if the active model's token ratio has been verified against historical usage, or 5% (ESTIMATE_RESERVE_UNCALIBRATED) otherwise. Finally, the function deducts the cumulative reserve from max_tokens and applies a hard floor of max_tokens // 2, ensuring that prompt allocations never collapse below half the context window even under severe reservation constraints.

Parameters:

  • max_tokens (int): Total context window capacity for the target model.
  • thinking_level (str | None, optional): The active reasoning effort tier (e.g., "low", "medium", "high"), used to look up thinking token reserves. Defaults to None.

Returns:

  • int: The maximum allowed prompt token capacity.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions internally.

Example:

# Invocation pattern from codebase pipeline nodes
budget = input_token_budget(max_tokens=128_000, thinking_level="high")

docs.title: count_tokens_raw()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def count_tokens_raw(text: str) -> int:

Description: Calculates the raw, uncalibrated token count for a text string using tiktoken's cl100k_base encoding. Strings shorter than MEMO_MIN_CHARS (256 characters) are encoded directly without caching overhead. For larger strings, it computes a lookup key tuple (len(text), hash(text)) and checks the thread-safe _memo cache before executing BPE encoding.

Parameters:

  • text (str): The raw text string to count.

Returns:

  • int: The token count measured against cl100k_base (or the UTF-8 fallback approximation).

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions; encoding loading errors are trapped and degrade to byte-level estimation.

Example:

# Extracted from utils/token_utils.py:131-143
def count_tokens_raw(text: str) -> int:
    """tiktoken cl100k_base token count (no model calibration). Memoized by content."""
    if not text:
        return 0
    if len(text) < MEMO_MIN_CHARS:
        return _encode_count(text)
    key = (len(text), hash(text))
    cached = _memo_get(key)
    if cached is not None:
        return cached
    count = _encode_count(text)
    _memo_put(key, count)
    return count

The function handles empty strings early by returning zero. When strings meet the size threshold, it queries _memo_get using a composite key of length and precomputed string hash; on cache misses, it computes the token count via _encode_count and updates the cache via _memo_put.

docs.title: count_tokens_raw_many()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def count_tokens_raw_many(texts: list[str]) -> list[int]:

Description: Computes raw token counts for an iterable of text strings, utilizing the memoization cache for known entries and multi-threaded parallel batch encoding for uncached entries.

docs.title: Phase 1: Cache Inspection and Batch Assembly
docs.text:
counts = [0] * len(texts)
    pending = []
    for i, text in enumerate(texts):
        if not text:
            continue
        key = (len(text), hash(text)) if len(text) >= MEMO_MIN_CHARS else None
        cached = _memo_get(key) if key else None
        if cached is not None:
            counts[i] = cached
        else:
            pending.append((i, text, key))

An output array pre-populated with zeros is instantiated alongside a pending list. Each string is inspected; empty strings remain zero, qualifying cached strings are resolved immediately via _memo_get, and cache misses (or short strings) are queued into pending along with their original index and memo key.

docs.title: Phase 2: Multi-Threaded Batch Encoding and Fallback
docs.text:
enc = _get_encoding()
    if pending and enc is not None:
        encoded = enc.encode_ordinary_batch([text for _, text, _ in pending], num_threads=min(8, os.cpu_count() or 1))
        results = [len(tokens) for tokens in encoded]
    else:
        results = [_fallback_count(text) for _, text, _ in pending]

If uncached strings exist and tiktoken is operational, the function dispatches them to enc.encode_ordinary_batch, capping thread concurrency to $\min(8, \text{cpu_count})$. If the tokenizer failed to load, it processes each pending item sequentially through _fallback_count.

docs.title: Phase 3: Cache Storage and Result Synthesis
docs.text:
for (i, _text, key), count in zip(pending, results, strict=True):
        counts[i] = count
        if key:
            _memo_put(key, count)
    return counts

The resulting token lengths are mapped back to their original ordinal slots in counts. For any item possessing a valid cache key, _memo_put records the result in the LRU cache.

Parameters:

  • texts (list[str]): A sequence of text strings to tokenize.

Returns:

  • list[int]: Parallel list of raw token counts corresponding to the input texts.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions internally.

Example:

# Invocation pattern for processing repository files in batch
file_contents = ["def alpha(): pass", "def beta(): pass"]
raw_counts = count_tokens_raw_many(file_contents)

Signature: def calibration_enabled() -> bool:

Description: Checks whether dynamic tokenizer ratio calibration is active. It inspects the TOKEN_RATIO_CALIBRATION environment variable, defaulting to enabled (True) unless explicitly set to "off", "0", "false", or "no" (case-insensitive).

Parameters:
